query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A defect‐aware machine‐learning model trained on binary-metal and high-entropy alloy datasets, which explicitly incorporates the effects of 1 wt.% oxygen contamination and point defects, will predict the temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than traditional analytical models based on perfect-crystal assumptions.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy, with a controlled oxygen contamination level of approximately 1 wt.% (introducing point defects and local lattice distortions).
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a machine-learning predictive framework that is trained on binary alloy and HEA datasets including defect and oxygen contamination data, rather than solely on defect-free, ideal crystalline simulations.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated in two temperature regimes: a low-temperature regime (0–200 K) where quantum effects and defect scattering are prominent, and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) where thermal disorder and oxidation effects become significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen-induced point defects and associated lattice distortions that alter electron scattering and phonon transport mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating defect and oxygen impurity effects into the ML model, the approach accounts for real-sample imperfections that lead to modifications in the conduction paths (e.g., increased scattering), thereby reducing the discrepancy between idealized analytical predictions and experimental observations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The defect-aware ML model will yield conductivity predictions with a reduced error margin relative to traditional models. In particular, the model is expected to more accurately capture the drop in conductivity at low temperatures due to defect-induced scattering as well as the more complex behavior at high temperatures arising from oxygen-related oxidation processes.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions that assume a perfect, defect-free crystal structure, which typically exhibit notable deviations from experimental measurements in oxygen-contaminated samples.
generation.boundary: Applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen contamination up to approximately 1 wt.% and within the temperature range of 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Predictions outside these oxygen or temperature limits remain unverified.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy is uncertain, as it depends on the representativeness and quality of the training data from binary systems and HEAs. Furthermore, the magnitude of defect-related scattering effects as a function of temperature may introduce additional uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with a controlled oxygen concentration near 1 wt.%. Measure their electrical conductivity over two temperature intervals (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) using standard four-probe methods. Independently, use the developed defect-aware ML model to predict the conductivity across the same temperature ranges for these samples. The experimental measurements should be performed on samples whose microstructural features (e.g., defect density and oxygen distribution) are characterized via microscopy and spectroscopic techniques.
measurements: Electrical conductivity (or resistivity) across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Microstructural characterization to verify oxygen content and defect distribution (e.g., TEM, XRD, and possibly atom probe tomography).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the defect-aware ML model’s predictions differ from the experimentally measured conductivity values by more than a pre-specified error threshold (e.g., >20% deviation) consistently across either temperature regime, or if the model fails to capture the qualitative trends (e.g., the conductivity drop at low temperatures due to defect scattering) observed in experiments, then the hypothesis that the approach improves accuracy over traditional models will be falsified.

This task is not possible currently, for the reasons discussed in the introduction. Using knowledge gained from on-going research it is possible to make some informed predictions for the selected alloys. The latter and the calculated (predicted) properties can be tested experimentally. For example, the alloy A should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3 and Nbss should be stable at 1500 °C but not the C14 NbCr2 Laves and A15 intermetallic phases and the alloy should not pest. The alloy B should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, eutectic with Nbss and Nb5Si3 should form (see below), in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3, Nbss (most likely solid solution with no Si) and A15 intermetallic should be stable at 1500 °C but not C14 NbCr2 Laves phase and the alloy should not pest.

The diffusion distance of Hf in Nb is ≈18 µm and 31µm, respectively after 100 and 300 h at 1500 °C.

Ti-rich oxide was not found in the scales formed at 800 °C and also was not found in the scale formed on the alloy ZX5 at 1200 °C, which would suggest that Cr promoted the formation of this oxide only at 1200 °C. The average oxygen concentration in the oxides was close to that in NbO2 (66.7 at.%), TiO2 (66.7 at.%), and Nb2O5 (71.4 at.%) and could be considered to be mixtures of TiO2 and TiNb2O7 oxides []. The latter oxides have been identified in the scales formed on Nb-silicide-based alloys [,,]. The concentrations of elements in the oxide formed on the alloy ZX7 at 1200 °C were similar to those reported for the same oxide for the alloy JG6 at the same temperature []. The Sn concentration and the Nb + Ti sum were the same in the alloys ZX3 and ZX7.

The structure of the paper is as follows. First the approach used to design and select the two alloys is explained. Then the experimental techniques used for the characterisation of the alloys are described. The results for the cast and heat treated alloys are presented before their isothermal oxidation at 800 and 1200 °C is presented. The discussion considers first the macrosegregation and microstructures of the alloys, which are also compared with High Entropy Alloys, and then their oxidation behaviour is considered.

In summary, guided by the literature on the oxidation of intermetallic compounds, the alloy design methodology NICE, the available phase equilibria data and data about macrosegregation in Nb-Si based alloys, we selected two alloys, namely the alloys Nb1.7Si2.4Ti2.4Al3Hf0.5 and Nb1.3Si2.4Ti2.4Al3.5Hf0.4, which we wanted to have (i) zero vol.% Nbss and (ii) microstructures consisting of MexAly aluminides and MexSiy silicides, and form alumina scales at 800 and 1200 °C. Also, we were interested to find out if zones of different microstructures would form in these alloys.

To date, the alloying elements that have been considered by our group for possible BC alloys are Al, Cr, Fe, Hf, Nb, Si, and Ti [,,,] and the alloying with Fe has been identified as not desirable owing to concerns about liquation []. The remaining elements are all known to improve the oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide-based alloys []. Two more elements are known to improve the oxidation of the latter alloys, namely B and Ge, owing to their effects on phase selection and stability [,,,]. Furthermore, when the alloying behaviour of Nb-silicide-based alloys is considered, the B-containing alloys form their own group []. It is important for future research to find out how B or Ge would affect the oxidation of BC alloys and the location of such alloys in maps of the parameters δ, Δχ, and VEC.

The ability to cast Nb-silicide-based alloys is a great advantage over other RMICs []. However, owing to their very high liquidus temperatures, cold hearth processing is required, and macrosegregation can be severe in these materials depending on alloying additions []. Tin, Ge, or B have a strong effect on macrosegregation [,,,,]. The additions of Sn or Ge, which can play a key role in the suppression of pest oxidation [,,,,,,,], can also reduce the alloy liquidus temperature, depending on their concentration and other alloying elements, for example, Al, Cr, Hf, Mo, and Ti. It is believed that their role in the alloy to achieve a balance of mechanical and oxidation properties depends on their concentration in the alloy. For example, it was suggested [,] that Sn can be effective at concentrations up to 2 at.% and that, at this “low” content, the A15-Nb3Sn compound is not stable. The (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti)B2 material was chosen for detailed high-pressure, high-temperature investigation because it is known to have the best thermal oxidation resistance of all the known transition metal borides up to 1200 °C [], and our preliminary mechanical property measurements indicate that (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Zr)B2 has a high hardness value amongst HEB materials. In this study, we present a novel experimental approach where HEB material is synthesized under high pressures and high temperatures and its crystal structure and compressibility are studied under extreme environments in the same sample chamber without exposing the sample to ambient conditions, thereby minimizing contamination and generating data on high-purity HEB materials.

Machine learning (ML) techniques have been actively utilized for various applications in recent years due to their superior prediction performance. However, as the applications expand vastly, they also have been required to meet the demand of high level of transparency and accountability due to their black-box framework. As a result, explainable ML methods have attracted a great deal of attention in order to further advance the reliability and applicability of ML-based approaches. Model explainability is also becoming increasingly important in the materials science domain as ML and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven algorithms are beginning to show success in simplifying various workflows. However, the idea of incorporating explainable ML methods into the current data-driven materials design and discovery workflow is still in its infancy. Unlike many other disciplines, materials science suffers from limited and sparse data. Incorporating interpretablility into the black-box ML models make it possible to explain the ML predictions with more confidence, especially when the models are trained using small and heterogeneous datasets. cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Contamination of Nb with Interstitials
cited_evidence.text: Oxygen contents as high as 0.41 wt.% increased the room temperature tensile strength of Nb from 276 MPa to 896 PMa and reduced the elongation from 30 to 10%. Contamination of Nb with oxygen increased its hardness [] and caused embrittlement [,]. The latter has been attributed to screw dislocations moving through a repulsive field imposed by oxygen atoms, forming cross kinks and emitting excess vacancies in Nb which bind with oxygen and hinder dislocation motion []. Oxygen also affected the elevated temperature properties []. Tensile tests conducted on Nb with varying oxygen concentrations (10, 200 and 4300 wppm) revealed brittle failures below 400 °C for oxygen concentration of 0.43% []. At higher temperatures ductile failures were produced. The amount of ductility exhibited by Nb−O alloys at elevated temperatures was sensitive to strain-rate. For example, Nb containing 0.15% oxygen exhibited a decrease in the reduction in area from 90% to 30% at 467 °C due to a change in strain rate of 5 × 10−5 to 2 × 10−1 s−1 [].

In RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, the CC bcc solid solutions with Ge+Sn and Al, Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti and W additions are (i) stable (Figure 1) and (ii) Si free [,]. It is suggested (a) that single phase bcc solid solution RCCAs or RHEAs with above elements would be stable at high temperatures. Furthermore, given that Ge+Sn with Al, Cr, Hf, Mo and Ti improve oxidation at pest and high temperatures [,,,] it is suggested (b) that these RCCAs or RHEAs would also be oxidation resistant. For B containing RM(Nb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, RM(NB)ICs/RHEAs, RCCAs and RHEAs it is suggested to study the contamination with oxygen of their solid solutions and to find out if there is a relationship between the parameter δ and the oxygen concentration, see Boron Containing RM(Nb)ICs in Section 3.2.1.

reading.lever: Develop a defect-aware ML model trained on binary and HEA datasets to predict conductivity in oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr over broad temperature ranges.
reading.why: It leverages proven ML techniques from related systems to incorporate defect and oxygen effects, addressing the perfect-crystal limitation of current analytical predictions.
